tagline: A swimming millstone that dives for jellies
summary: One of the heaviest bony fishes on Earth: a huge, flattened disc with towering fins and no proper tail, able to top 2.5 tonnes. Once thought to be a lazy drifter, it is an active swimmer that dives hundreds of metres to hunt jellies and siphonophores, then returns toward the surface.
ability: wing-like fin flapping and deep dives

stats.size: Up to about 3.3 m long and 4.2 m tall fin-to-fin; over 2.5 tonnes
stats.depth: Mostly the top 200 m; dives beyond 800 m, possibly 1,000 m
stats.diet: Jellyfish, siphonophores, salps and comb jellies; also small crustaceans, squids and fishes

facts.title: A fish without a tail
facts.text: Instead of a tail fin it has a clavus—Latin for 'rudder'—a stiff lobe formed from extensions of the dorsal and anal fins. Its name Mola is Latin for millstone, after its round shape.

facts.title: Flying underwater
facts.text: It swims by flapping its tall dorsal and anal fins in unison, like a pair of wings. This is thought to be an efficient stroke that lets it dive repeatedly to great depths.

facts.title: Not just a lazy drifter
facts.text: Tagged sunfish in the north-west Atlantic spent over 80% of their time in the top 200 m but dived as deep as 844 m, making regular forays to feed on deep-water siphonophores and jellies.

facts.title: Why bask at the surface?
facts.text: Sunfish are often seen lying flat at the surface. One idea is that they warm up after cold dives; but a tagging study found no link between cold-water time and surface time, so the reason remains debated.

facts.title: 300 million eggs
facts.text: A single adult female can produce up to 300 million tiny, buoyant eggs, yet sunfish larvae are rarely collected.

image.alt: A huge, flat, disc-shaped fish with a tall fin above and below hangs in green water over a rocky wreck, while two scuba divers work on the seabed below it.
image.caption: A large ocean sunfish buzzes NOAA divers documenting the wreck of the schooner Paul Palmer, Stellwagen Bank National Marine Sanctuary, Massachusetts, 2006.
image.creator: Matthew Lawrence, Stellwagen Bank NMS, NOS, NOAA

notes: Image chosen from Stellwagen Bank (NW Atlantic), where Mola mola is the expected species; images from the Galápagos, Namibia/South Africa and unspecified locations were avoided because the look-alike Mola alexandrini and M. tecta occur in the Southern Hemisphere. Commons lists the file under both PD-USGov-NOAA and CC BY 2.0 (NOAA Flickr); public domain recorded. Divers appear in the frame (gives scale). 'Heaviest bony fish' is avoided: the sources call M. mola the heaviest/largest bony fish, but the heaviest recorded individual (Azores, 2021) has been reported as Mola alexandrini (from memory of Sawai et al. 2022; not re-verified in this session)—worded as 'one of the heaviest'. Fact refs: 'not a lazy drifter' combines the Potter & Howell (2010) tagging figures quoted by the Australian Museum with Fishes of Australia's note on siphonophore-feeding dives. Depth gauge max uses the 844 m tagging record; Fishes of Australia mentions records beyond 1,000 m. 'Reproduction' category based on extreme fecundity.
